# Commercial Arithmetic

## Core ideas and reasoning

Percentages compare a change with a stated base. Profit percentage is usually profit divided by cost price, while profit margin uses selling price; read the wording. A discount reduces marked price by a fraction of that price. Simple interest I = Prt uses the original principal throughout, with rate r as a decimal per time period. Compound amount A = P(1+r)ⁿ applies interest to the growing balance; depreciation uses P(1-r)ⁿ. Keep the rate and number of periods consistent. Hire purchase cost is deposit plus all instalments; compare it with cash price to find extra cost. Currency conversions use the stated buying or selling rate from the institution's point of view. For taxation, apply each tax rate only to the portion of taxable income in that band, then apply any specified relief. Distinguish gross and net income. Check commercial calculations by reversing the multiplier; a 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease does not return to the original amount because the bases differ.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

An article costs KSh 800 and sells for KSh 1000. Find the profit percentage on cost.

Profit = 1000 - 800 = KSh 200. Percentage = 200/800 × 100 = 25%. Profit margin on sales would instead be 20%.

### Example 2

Find simple interest on KSh 20000 at 6% per year for 3 years.

I = 20000 × 0.06 × 3 = KSh 3600. Total amount = KSh 23600. Annual interest is KSh 1200, checking three years gives KSh 3600.

### Example 3

KSh 10000 is invested at 10% compound interest per year for 2 years. Find the amount.

A = 10000(1.1)² = KSh 12100. Year one gives 11000; year two adds 1100. Interest earned is KSh 2100.

### Example 4

A machine worth KSh 50000 depreciates by 20% each year. Find its value after 2 years.

Value = 50000(0.8)² = KSh 32000. Sequentially: 40000 after year one and 32000 after year two.

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
